Progressives and moderates rejoice: 6 takeaways from the midterms

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1043 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries addresses an election night watch party in Washington on Tuesday after Democrats were projected to win the House.
  • Democrats were savoring their midterm election rout Wednesday after decisively flipping both the House and Senate.
  • It has been revealed that “Last night was beyond even our largest expectations of what could happen,” Arizona Rep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries addresses an election night watch party in Washington on Tuesday after Democrats were projected to win the House. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Democrats were savoring their midterm election rout Wednesday after decisively flipping both the House and Senate.

It has been revealed that “Last night was beyond even our largest expectations of what could happen,” Arizona Rep. Greg Stanton noted on a press call.

Hakeem Jeffries, the top House Democrat in line to become the first Black speaker, predicted Democrats would hold at least 255 seats next year, which would be the largest majority for either party since Democrats won 257 seats in 2008.

In the Senate, the Democratic Caucus was poised to hold at least 54 seats after seismic red-state gains, with two key races too close to call.

Industry observers note that “What we have now seen is a generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America not only now but on into the future,” Charles E. Schumer, the chamber’s top Democrat, said Wednesday.

Here are six takeaways from the midterm elections:.

Sources indicate that democratic gains were so sweeping that both ideological wings of the party had plenty to celebrate. The moderate Blue Dogs more than doubled their current membership, with at least 22 Blue Dog PAC-endorsed candidates winning Tuesday. Meanwhile, the Congressional Progressive Caucus anticipated at least 25 new members.

For House progressives, swing-seat wins in Michigan and California were signs that their candidates’ message resonated in battleground races and that Democrats should move to implement those progressive ideas next year.

“Massive majorities can get big things done,” Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Greg Casar said on a Wednesday press call.

Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider, the chair of the center-left Latest Democrat Coalition, told reporters he had a strong relationship with Casar and envisioned different factions of the party working together.

Industry observers note that “It doesn’t matter what you call your idea. If your idea is going to help us move the ball forward, join us at the table,” Schneider noted.

Army veteran Cait Conley, who was leading GOP Rep. Mike Lawler in a race that remained uncalled Wednesday afternoon, remarked she’d been open about having differences with incoming Newly introduced York Democrats aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America. But she said Democrats across the political spectrum needed to prioritize “real solutions for the American people.”.

“If we don’t make that our priority, if we don’t show that that is more important than anything else … then I think the voters are going to show us in 2028 that they’re not going to accept that,” she noted on the Latest Dems press call.

While the president cast a shadow over the entire midterm map, three of his marquee candidates were among the night’s biggest busts.

Sources indicate that trump was behind appointed South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham every step of the way, helping her win a contested primary to replace her late brother, Lindsey Graham, on the ballot. But Graham lost to Democrat Annie Andrews in a stunning upset. In North Carolina, Trump had publicly urged Michael Whatley to run for the state’s open seat. But the former Republican National Committee chairman lost to Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper by 20 points. And most significantly, in Texas, Trump elevated scandal-plagued state Attorney General Ken Paxton over Republican incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. But the president’s support wasn’t enough to stave off a general election drubbing at the hands of Democrat James Talarico.

Even Rep. Julia Letlow, Trump’s pick for Senate in deep-red Louisiana, won her election by less than 2 points.

Republicans in seven states successfully embarked on a mid-decade redistricting spree aimed at boosting GOP candidates. But the push couldn’t overcome the political headwinds that battered the Republican brand. In California, where Democrats debuted a redistricting push in response to the Texas redraw, the latest map proved more beneficial: Democrats are poised to flip at least four seats they redrew in their favor.

Recent findings suggest that republican Alex Mealer was the heavy favorite to win a redrawn Houston-area seat that Trump would have carried by 20 points. She raised $2.8 million to first-time Democratic candidate Leticia Gutierrez’ $215,000. Yet Gutierrez won the contest by double digits. In an interview on MS NOW, Gutierrez mentioned her campaign proved that “you don’t need money to buy a congressional race.” She wasn’t the only under-the-radar House contender to pull off an unexpected victory Tuesday. In North Carolina, several low-profile and under-funded Democrats appear poised to pull off unlikely upsets, though the races remain too close to call.

Democrats have chased the dream of a blue Texas for more than 30 years — and always came up short. Until Tuesday. The party notched a series of stunning wins in the nation’s most consequential red state — from Talarico’s decisive victory in the Senate contest to winning several key House races to capturing the governor’s mansion. Democrats seized every elected statewide position on the ballot and flipped the state House, according to The Associated Press. “They stated it could not be done,’’ Democratic Rep. Christian Menefee told supporters Tuesday night. “We did it.”.

Recent findings suggest that democrats made deep gains in red states and districts across the country, flipping Senate seats in Texas, South Carolina and Kansas, while races in Alaska and Mississippi remained too close to call. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis called it “probably the political worst case scenario for a midterm election.”.

But Democrats didn’t appear convinced that their brand had completely rebounded from deep losses two years ago, saying they had work to do over the next two years.

“Many of the folks who voted for us yesterday, of course, are still skeptical,” Schumer mentioned.

In a recent development, similarly, Casar and Rep. Pramila Jayapal both warned Democrats not to assume that Tuesday’s wins had resolved the party’s branding issues.

In a recent development, “We still are not particularly popular as a Democratic Party across the country,” Jayapal told reporters. “I think we’ve got a shot to show that we can deliver on the kind of bold populist change that people ran on and won on.”.

Nina Heller contributed to this report.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that former Ohio Sen.
  • Even in an election cycle marked by surprises and upsets, Capitol Hill observers will spot some familiar faces (identical twins notwithstanding) among this year’s midterm winners.
  • At least seven former members won comeback bids Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, here at a Oct. 20 campaign event near Ohio University in Athens, won his comeback bid Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Even in an election cycle marked by surprises and upsets, Capitol Hill observers will spot some familiar faces (identical twins notwithstanding) among this year’s midterm winners.

At least seven former members won comeback bids Tuesday.

In a recent development, the winners included alumni who dusted themselves off after election losses just two years ago. But other winners haven’t been in office in nearly two decades, their service predating the addition of a women’s restroom in the House (more recent than you may guess).

Here’s how these former members did on election night:.

Carl lost a primary to fellow Republican Rep. Barry Moore in 2024 after a upcoming map placed them in the same district. But with Moore running for the Senate in 2026, Carl had an easier path back to his old seat, which was redrawn again this year. He defeated his Democratic opponent Tuesday by 18 points.

According to recent reports, it has been nearly two decades since Solis last served in Congress. She left in 2009 to serve as President Barack Obama’s first Labor secretary. Solis was in her sixth term as a Los Angeles county supervisor when she announced a bid for Congress after California voters approved a map that created five Democratic pickup opportunities.

According to recent reports, solis faced limited resistance on her path to victory in the 38th District, especially after Democratic Rep. Linda T. Sánchez opted to run for the redrawn 41st District.

Bean is making her way back to the House after losing her suburban Chicagoland seat in the conservative tea party wave of 2010.

Industry observers note that A decade-and-a-half later, she won an eight-way primary for the 8th District seat Democrat Raja Krishnamoorthi vacated for an unsuccessful Senate bid. Winning the nomination all but guaranteed Bean a November victory in the deep-blue seat.

In a recent development, one of the cycle’s biggest comeback stories was in the Buckeye State, where Sherrod Brown was mounting a bid two years after Republican Bernie Moreno had unseated him. Positioning himself as an opponent of data centers, Brown defeated appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in a special election for the remainder of now Vice President JD Vance’s term. He could take office as early as December but would have to run again in 2028 if he wants another full term.

It has been revealed that first elected in 2018, Allred left Congress two years ago after an unsuccessful Senate campaign against Republican incumbent Ted Cruz. After briefly launching a second Senate bid, Allred switched to a redrawn open House seat and won his primary over Rep. Julie Elizabeth Johnson, his successor in the chamber. Allred had no trouble winning his general election Tuesday for a fourth House term.

McAdams served one term in Congress representing a battleground Utah seat, before being unseated by Republican Burgess Owens in 2020. But after a state judge approved a latest congressional map that created a heavily Democratic seat anchored in Salt Lake City, McAdams jumped into the race. He comfortably won his primary over more progressive opponents and stomped his way to a second term on Tuesday.

Once a high-ranking member of the House Armed Services Committee, Luria lost her Hampton Roads seat in 2022 to Republican Jen Kiggans.

But a week after Virginia Democrats posted strong showings in the commonwealth’s 2025 off-year elections, Luria debuted her House comeback bid and went on to oust Kiggans on Tuesday.

Industry observers note that former House Intelligence Chairman Mike Rogers left the House after the 2014 elections and made his first Senate bid 10 years later. He lost to Democrat Elissa Slotkin but sought the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters the following year.

Recent findings suggest that rogers tried to take advantage of Democratic divisions between primary winner Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens, even winning a late endorsement from the congresswoman. But it was not enough to stop El-Sayed on Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that republican John E. Sununu served three terms in the House and one in the Senate before losing to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen in 2008. With Shaheen retiring, Sununu attempted a comeback but ended up losing decisively to Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas.

In a recent development, movado was founded in 1881 in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland, which isn’t a particularly odd backstory for a heritage Swiss watch brand. But it has been American owned since 1983 and has a distinct quality tied deeply to its long history in the U.S. market—which puts it slightly outside the predictable purview of many watch collectors.

Right now, a growing band of horological nerds is finding rich pickings in the Movado back catalog and pushing up vintage prices considerably—especially for its mid-century chronographs and its legendary Museum Watch (which celebrates 80 years in 2027; more of that to come) in the process.

In a recent development, it’s not only the collectors who are digging into Movado’s past, however. Last month, the brand released the Heritage Tempo-Matic ($995–$1,095), a re-creation of a watch that merges sporty and retro design in a neat and slinky package. The Tempo-Matic, Movado’s first automatic movement, was launched in 1945 and went on to power a broad range of Movado’s wristwatches. But the rounded yet boxy “TV” shape of the new Heritage Tempo-Matic is unmistakably 1970s, when watch design took a giant leap forward into sexy new territory.

The 2026 version is available in three executions, each powered by the reliable Sellita SW200-1B movement and fitted with integrated steel bracelets that positively scream seventies. Two of them come in brushed steel with vertically brushed burgundy or blue dials. A third—which, we must admit, is our favorite—is gold-tone PVD with a warm gray dial. You’d be hard-pressed to find such an elegant, authentic, and affordable homage to the 1970s—a decade that’s presently a very hot motif in watch-collecting circles—anywhere else.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you’re a country music fan (or tbh, even if you’re not), then you’re probably well aware that the love lives of country music’s rising stars are quite entangled…and have been for a minute now. The latest (reported) revision? Ella Langley and Tucker Wetmore are rumored to be dating, but we really can’t talk about their maybe-relationship without discussing Tucker’s ex Bryana Ferringer...or Ella’s rumored ex Riley Green (who went on to maybe date Bryana).

Industry observers note that ella and Tucker may have sparked dating rumors late last year, but it wasn’t without some drama on the way. It’s a pretty confusing ride, so buckle up and let’s get into it. Starting with….

In a recent development, after months of dating rumors following the success of Ella and Riley’s song “You Look Like You Love Me,” Ella finally shuts down Riley dating rumors. “We’re not dating,” she tells Taste of Country, adding, “We’re just good friends.”.

Sources indicate that riley also shuts down dating speculation during an appearance on The Viall Files podcast. “Ella’s probably too smart to date me anyway,” he jokes, later adding, “When we first started having the success we did with that song, I kinda told Ella, I was like, ‘There’s gonna be a lot of things mentioned, but I mean, you don’t really have to play into it or not play into it.’”.

Tucker posts a TikTok on August 20 with the caption “@ my ex,” sparking breakup rumors with his model girlfriend Bryana (who, btw, appeared in his music video for “Wind Up Missin’ You”).

Soon after, Bryana is spotted with Riley at his Red Rocks tour stop.

Ella and Tucker both attend the 2025 BMI Country Awards on November 18, though it’s unclear whether this is the first time they ever meet (or if they even interacted, despite standing right next to each other in this group photo):.

A day later, after several reported sightings around Nashville, Riley brings Bryana as his date to the CMA Awards on November 19.

However! Riley later refers to Bryana as merely a “friend,” telling Backstage Country, “It’s gonna be tough to tiptoe out of having a date to an award show. Yeah, I mean, you go to award shows all the time, and I’m always by myself, or I’ve got, like, a security guy, or a buddy with me, so I took a friend with me to the award show.”.

Industry observers note that around the same time, Ella sparks dating rumors with Farmer Wants a Wife season 3 star John Sansone (whose cousin, music exec Sophia Sansone, previously dated Riley). Rumors begin after John includes a picture of Ella’s dog, Crue, in a November 26 Instagram photo dump...and then, on the same day, Ella includes a video of herself shooting shotguns with John in a photo dump of her own.

John later confirms to Taste of Country in April 2026 that he and Ella “dated for a couple of months” after he slid into her DMs but are no longer together.

Oh, and side note: John’s ex from Farmer Wants a Wife, Samantha Riehl, posted a TikTok with Tucker back in April 2025 with the caption, “Blondes are the worst.”.

And then right after, John posted a TikTok with Bryana at Stagecoach (which has since been deleted).

Pretty sure nothing ever happened between Samantha and Tucker (or between Bryana and John), but still, it feels worth mentioning!!

On December 5, Tucker releases “Proving Me Right,” which fans are preeeetty convinced is about his ex, Bryana.

A few weeks later, Ella and Tucker are photographed together in the British Virgin Islands at the Soggy Dollar Bar...but considering the photo also includes other country artists, rumors circulate that the trip was possibly a writing retreat.

Tucker and Ella reunite to sing a live acoustic duet of Tucker’s “Sunburn” at the Heart Strings for Hope charity event on March 10.

And while Tucker didn’t write “Sunburn” himself, a few of the lyrics kiiiinda seem to allude to his December getaway with Ella.

Tucker then appears on the March 17 episode of Kristin Cavallari’s Let’s Be Honest podcast, where he claims that he has “never been broken up with” and has always been the one to “call it quits.” When Kristin asks if he has “sworn off blondes,” Tucker notes, “Yep. I have. For the foreseeable future. That’s right.”.

And then, a few days after that on March 21, Tucker posts an Instagram photo of himself holding a fish, and Ella slides into his comments with, “Cute fish.” Flirty!

Tucker discusses his hit “Brunette” with Audacy, saying, “My mom’s always mentioned, ‘You're going to mess around with blondes for a little while but I truly believe you're going to settle down with the brunette,’ and I was like, ‘Yeah, 100 percent.’”.

Not long after, during an appearance on Taste of Country Nights, Tucker notes, “Pretty much every girlfriend I have ever had was blonde, and I think it’s time to change up a couple of things.”.

On September 23 (just a day after Ella breaks Mariah Carey’s record for longest-running Billboard Hot 100 hit with “Choosin’ Texas”), TMZ breaks the news that Tucker and Ella are (reportedly) dating.

The outlet obtains photos of the two out with friends in Nashville on the night of September 22 following the Nashville Songwriter Awards, with sources telling TMZ that the two met “through the music industry and mutual friends.”.

Multiple sources also confirm the rumored romance to People so…it seems legit to me!

While making an appearance at WAVE in Wichita, Kansas, a fan straight-up asks Tucker whether he and Ella “are a thing.”.

Recent findings suggest that tucker’s two-word response? “Next question.” Okay!!

Ella and Tucker seemingly take another trip to the Virgin Islands…at least, according to a sneaky fan who spotted them entering a restaurant together.

Recent findings suggest that soon after, they attend the CMAs, where they walk the carpet separately but still can’t dodge questions about their relationship status. When asked by People if there is a certain brunette he’s rooting for, he jokingly answers, “Zach Top or Stephen Wilson Jr.” Mmmkay!

Ella is also caught grinning during Tucker’s performance, which...isn’t confirmation of anything but certainly telling.

The incoming freshman class of the 120th Congress includes several people who scored historic wins in their states and the nation at large.

Among them were women breaking glass ceilings in the Senate and trailblazers for Native American representation. Beyond Washington, a handful of nominees pulled off milestone victories in gubernatorial elections, including four Black candidates. Congress is also poised to witness history next year with New York Democrat Hakeem Jeffries expected to become the first Black speaker.

Here are some of the candidates who made history on election night, both in Congress and in the governor's mansions:.

Alfonso, the son-in-law of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, is the first Gen Z Republican elected to Congress with his victory in Wisconsin’s open 7th District, a seat his father-in-law once held.

Andrews, a pediatrician, becomes the first woman elected to the Senate from South Carolina after defeating appointed Republican incumbent Darline Graham, the first female senator from the Palmetto State.

With her victory in New York’s 13th District, Avila Chevalier becomes the first Muslim person elected to Congress from the Empire State. She succeeds Democratic Rep. Adriano Espaillat, whom she defeated in the primary.

Benitez-Thompson, a former majority leader of the Nevada State Assembly, is the first Democrat elected to represent the state’s 2nd District since its creation after the 1980 census.

With his victory over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, Colom, a district attorney, will be Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction. He will also be the Magnolia State’s first Black senator elected directly by voters.

Conely, a Navy veteran, unseats Republican Rep. Mike Lawler to become the first openly gay woman elected to Congress from New York.

Industry observers note that dandiya, the daughter of Indian immigrants, becomes the first South Asian American elected to Congress from Florida with her victory in the redrawn 22nd District. She is also one of the first adherents of Jainism to be elected to Congress, along with Arizona's Amish Shah (see below).

With his victory over Republican Mike Rogers, El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, becomes the first Muslim person elected to the Senate.

A member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, Flanagan becomes the first Native American woman elected to the Senate with her victory over Republican Michele Tafoya. The outgoing Minnesota lieutenant governor is also the first Native American to represent the state in Congress.

Ford, a state senator, unseated Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz to become the first openly gay person elected to Congress from Indiana.

Hamawy, a former Army surgeon who emigrated from Egypt to the U.S. as an infant, is the first Muslim person elected to Congress from Latest Jersey, with his victory in the state’s 12th District.

Killin, an Army veteran and onetime chief of staff to former second gentleman Doug Emhoff, is the first Democrat elected to represent Colorado’s 5th District since its creation after the 1970 census.

Kiros, who upset Rep. Diana DeGette in the Democratic primary for Colorado’s 1st District, easily won the general election to become the first Black woman elected to Congress from the Centennial State. Kiros, who was born in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and emigrated to the U.S. as an infant, is also the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress.

According to recent reports, koh, the son of a Korean American father and a Lebanese American mother, is the first Asian American elected to Congress from Massachusetts. The former Biden administration alumnus will succeed Democrat Seth Moulton in the state’s 6th District.

It has been revealed that letlow, the first Republican woman elected to the House from Louisiana, earns the same distinction in the Senate with her victory over Democrat Jamie Davis in the open-seat race to succeed GOP Sen. Bill Cassidy.

It has been revealed that limtiaco will be the first Chamorro woman to represent Guam in Congress after she unseated Republican Del. James C. Moylan. She previously was the first woman to serve as U.S. attorney for the Districts of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands.

Recent findings suggest that mcCann, a state senator, defeated Republican Rep. Bill Huizenga to become the first Native American elected to Congress from Michigan. McCann is a member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation.

Moss, the president pro tempore of the Michigan Senate, keeps Rep. Haley Stevens’ 11th District in Democratic hands, becoming the first openly gay person elected to Congress from Michigan.

The grandson of a Mexican immigrant, Ojeda, who defeated National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson, is the first Latino elected to Congress from North Carolina.

By defeating former Sen. John E. Sununu, Pappas, a fourth-term congressman, becomes the first openly gay man elected to the Senate.

In a recent development, the daughter of immigrants from Chile and Cuba, Powell is the first Latino person elected to Congress from Nebraska after flipping the state’s 2nd District. She is also the first Democratic woman elected to Congress from Nebraska.

Sources indicate that unofficial returns show Sarauw winning the open-seat race to succeed outgoing Del. Stacey Plaskett, making her the first openly gay person elected to Congress from the U.S. Virgin Islands.

The son of Indian immigrants, Shah is the first South Asian American elected to Congress from Arizona. The former state legislator is also one of the first adherents of Jainism to be elected to Congress, along with Florida’s Pia Dandiya.

A citizen of the Ysleta del Sur Pueblo Nation, Valdez is the first Native American elected to Congress from Latest York. The New York State assemblywoman will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez.

Wiener, a state senator who succeeds former Speaker Nancy Pelosi in California’s 11th District, is the first openly gay person elected to represent San Francisco in Congress.

Sources indicate that with her victory over Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, Acton becomes the first woman elected governor of Ohio. Republican Nancy Hollister briefly served as the state’s top executive in the late 1990s but was never elected governor.

The son of Mexican immigrants, Becerra, a former congressman and Health and Human Services secretary, is the first Latino to be elected governor of California. He is the state’s second Latino governor after Romualdo Pacheco, who was never elected to the role but briefly succeeded an incumbent in 1875.

Blackburn, Tennessee’s first female senator, will soon become the Volunteer State’s first female governor after her victory over Democrat Jerri Green.

Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, will be the first Black person elected governor of Wisconsin after he defeated Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany.

Recent findings suggest that republican Rep. Byron Donalds will become Florida's first Black governor after he defeated Democrat David Jolly, a former GOP congressman.

Ford, the current Nevada attorney general, will become his state’s first Black governor after defeating Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo.

Industry observers note that haaland, a member of the Pueblo of Laguna, will become the first Native American woman to be elected governor in the U.S. after defeating Republican Gregg Hull. The former Interior secretary was also one of the first Native American women elected to Congress, along with Kansas Rep. Sharice Davids, in 2018.

Hinojosa, a state representative, will become the first Hispanic person elected Texas governor since statehood after she unseated three-term Republican incumbent Greg Abbott.

Klobuchar, the first woman to be elected senator from Minnesota, makes history again with her election as her state’s first female governor.

With her victory over Republican businessman Rick Jackson, Lance Bottoms becomes the first woman to be elected governor of Georgia. The former Atlanta mayor is also the state’s first Black governor and the first Black woman to be elected governor anywhere in the country, along with Del. Stacey Plaskett in the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Unofficial returns show Plaskett, the nonvoting delegate from the U.S. Virgin Islands, becoming the first woman to be elected governor of the island territory. She is also one of the first Black women to be elected governor in the country, along with Lance Bottoms in Georgia.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, as a certified holistic health coach and wellness content creator, Carolina Salazar knows the importance of a peaceful wind-down routine before bed. She trusts Hubspace from The Home Depot that powers many of the smart devices in her home, to help ease her into a good night’s sleep.

It has been revealed that hubspace, The Home Depot’s exclusive smart home platform, powers more than 250 products across select private brands—like Hampton Bay, Husky, and Vissani—as well as national brand partners. It effortlessly connects everyday essentials, including smart security, indoor and outdoor lighting, appliances, switches, watering controls, and more.

Some of the Hubspace app’s most practical features help people personalize lighting and improve home security. Hubspace Connect, for example, lets you control compatible lighting from a single switch, while Vacation Mode is a security feature that turns lights and smart plugs on and off while you’re away. One of Salazar’s favorite features is Circadian Rhythm, which automatically transitions lights from cooler, whiter tones to warmer ones as the day goes on.

“I can set my lights to follow my circadian rhythm, so they shift automatically throughout the day,” indicates Salazar. “And when they start to turn warm in the evening, that’s my cue to slow it down.” That can mean cozying up with a book, brewing a cup of hot tea, or, in her case, lighting a candle at her bedside and journaling. When Salazar is finished putting her thoughts to paper, she uses the Hubspace app to adjust the color, temperature, and brightness of her lights, dimming them as she gets closer to sleep. This can even be programmed automatically in order to reduce screen time before bed.

“Colder rooms bring better sleep, so I also have Hubspace turn on my AC at night,” she claims.

Sources indicate that the Hubspace app is free to download and easily syncs with your home’s smart devices. You can enable voice control for screen-free commands—also a plus if you’re trying to reduce your pre-sleep screen time. And the app runs on both WiFi and Bluetooth—so even if the WiFi is down, your nighttime routine can still run seamlessly.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, cantrall, who is perhaps best known for portraying Red, daughter of the Queen of Hearts, in the Descendants film series, has had a banner year.
  • At the show, Cantrall played four tracks, including “Carrie Bradshaw.” She took pictures with her fans, signed vinyls, and, for one fan, even signed their chest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that last night at the Moxy Downtown Los Angeles, rising pop star Kylie Cantrall teased her next project. “It’s gaggy. It’s giving 21,” she joked onstage during a small, intimate performance. “I actually haven’t written any ballads so far. I’m healed.”.

In a recent development, cantrall, who is perhaps best known for portraying Red, daughter of the Queen of Hearts, in the Descendants film series, has had a banner year. The L.A. native just wrapped a nationwide tour, appeared on Fox’s The Masked Singer, is set to perform at iHeart’s Jingle Ball, and dropped her EP Valley Girl Problems. A standout on the release is “Carrie Bradshaw,” which examines the similarities between Cantrall and the iconic Sex and the City character, played by Sarah Jessica Parker. “I think my fashion sense has been influenced by Carrie,” Cantrall says. “Also, she’s just kind of a mess, but she keeps it together on the outside. That’s honestly how I feel about myself. The choices are questionable, sometimes. Choices in dating, questionable.”.

At the show, Cantrall played four tracks, including “Carrie Bradshaw.” She took pictures with her fans, signed vinyls, and, for one fan, even signed their chest. The experience is a part of a larger effort to use music as a connector at the Moxy, which has also hosted Ayra Starr at its London property. The brand unites artists with their fans in private settings and gives travelers the opportunity to relax with a musical backdrop. “I’m so excited to be here at Moxy,” Cantrall told ELLE before taking the stage. “I love doing these little underplays and acoustic shows, because it’s a different side of myself that I feel like people don’t usually get to see.”.

Ahead of her performance, Cantrall sat down with ELLE to discuss Valley Girl Problems, her acoustic set, and upcoming music on the horizon.

Full production, dancers, props. It’s always very razzle-dazzle, Kylie the performer, but I feel like this is more Kylie just the singer and songwriter. I like getting to showcase that aspect.

Sources indicate that honestly, I get nervous for it all. I think I put so much thought and care into every show, so there’s always a pressure I put on myself. But I feel like once I get out there and see the cuties’ faces, it feels chill. I know so many of them. We have more of a friendship bond.

Sources indicate that it’s everything. What’s really special about me and my fan base is that we’ve really grown up together, because a lot of them are my age now. They had maybe started watching me from YouTube or from my first Disney show when I was 13 and have stayed along with my journey. It’s crazy. Our bond is kind of familial at this point.

Industry observers note that I think they’re quite different. It’s so different playing a character. Of course, with someone like Red, I’m very grateful I got to play a character that I felt like had a lot of me in it already. But, Kylie the musician, Kylie the artist, that’s completely, 100 percent raw me. I have so much freedom to take risks and experiment. With Valley Girl, I feel like that perfectly encapsulated the person I was a couple months ago when I wrote it. I’ve changed so much since then. I’m just excited for the next project that’s going to reflect who I am now as a 21-year-old. I want all of my bodies of work to reflect the person I am in whatever chapter that is. It’s like a time machine. It’s very powerful in that way.

No. I listen to it so much when I’m creating it, and obviously it’s just nonstop before it comes out. The minute it comes out, it feels like I have no control over it whatsoever. It’s not mine. It’s for everyone else. I have to have that kind of separation. If I am still listening to it after it’s been out, I’ll start to pick things apart and be like, “Oh, I wish I did that. Oh, I could have done this differently.” Then, you have people’s criticism or opinions also in your brain when you’re listening to it, which can taint the way you view it. I was so proud when I finished it. I knew how I felt once I submitted it to the label and was like, “Okay, this is the final product. Here you go.” I just want to remain in that place.

Recent findings suggest that it’s always the vocal fry—holding the ends of my words for a long time. Definitely the way I talk. I guess hiking and matcha are also kind of a worldwide thing at this point, but for some reason growing up I always felt like that’s such a Valley thing. In the Valley, it’s either matcha cafes or Pilates studios and fruit carts on the corner, and that kind of encapsulates the Valley for me.

According to recent reports, so excited. At the top of the year, I wrote in my little manifestation journal, I’m going to perform at Jingle Ball this holiday. It was before it was even a topic of conversation. I just threw it out there because I was like, I really want to do Jingle Ball just to be a part of a lineup. I’ve watched every single Jingle Ball since I was seven years old. The fact that I’ll get to share the stage with Katseye, Olivia [Rodrigo], the Jonas Brothers, Adéla, these are all artists that I look up to. I’m just excited to be in that orbit.

Recent findings suggest that I was probably enjoying my days off for the first two days when I got back home from tour. Then, the third day I was like, “Okay, I’m ready to get back out.” I’m already thinking in my head what the latest set list is going to be with the new songs that I’m recording at home right now and getting ready for the next album. My wheels are turning.

New York had a crazy energy. The New Yorkers know how to pull up and show some love. And, of course, L.A. I got to end the tour here, so there was something that felt very full circle about getting to come home and celebrate with my friends and family that all came out to the show, and a lot of my L.A. fans who are here tonight at the Moxy. It’s also just so fun anytime I get to do anything in L.A. It’s all my closest fans, and all my first pop-ups I had ever done were always here in L.A. A lot of my foundational fans that have been with me, they’re all here.

According to recent reports, I’m just taking a lot of inspiration from my life right now, as a 21-year-old who’s going out and just kind of embracing this next chapter. It feels like I have all the freedom in the world. I’m just excited to kind of show people maybe a little more of a wilder side. A little more messy, a little less curated. Kylie, outside of the work I’ve done or the image, the narrative, whatever that may be. Here’s who I am right now. I like to have fun. I like to go out. I’m going through it all the time, but I get to pour it into my music, whether it’s just discovering my kind of identity in this era, dating, or all the things I’m learning about myself. It’s all going to be poured into this record.

I’m a Cancer. I’m very in touch with my emotions at all times, and music is my chance to fully just, without censoring anything, explore that.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Why Travis Kelce Didn’t Join Taylor Swift at the 2026 CMA Awards

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (482 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Taylor Swift returned to the CMA Awards for the first time in 10 years this evening, but her husband, Travis Kelce, wasn’t seen there with her.
  • In a recent development, kelce is in the middle of his football season.
  • In a recent development, this past weekend, Kelce left the field for part of the team’s game against the Atlanta Falcons due to an ankle injury.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taylor Swift returned to the CMA Awards for the first time in 10 years this evening, but her husband, Travis Kelce, wasn’t seen there with her. Though the singer posed on the red carpet solo, she wasn’t alone during the ceremony—she was spotted beside her friend Brittany Mahomes, a fellow Kansas City Chiefs WAG. (She is married to Kelce’s teammate Patrick Mahomes, and they’re expecting their fourth child together.).

In a recent development, kelce is in the middle of his football season. His next game is at Arrowhead Stadium on Sunday, against the Arizona Cardinals, which could explain his absence this evening.

In a recent development, this past weekend, Kelce left the field for part of the team’s game against the Atlanta Falcons due to an ankle injury. Postgame, he gave USA Today an update. “I’m all good,” he remarked. “I probably could have went more than I did when I came back, but it was the direction the team wanted to go, so I was right there with them. We had a lot of young guys step up, so it was really nice.”.

Industry observers note that while he and Swift are supportive of each other’s careers, the pair hasn’t made their red carpet debut at an awards ceremony yet. Last March, they attended the iHeartRadio Music Awards together but skipped the red carpet. Kelce remained by Swift’s side throughout the show.

It has been revealed that in an October 2025 episode of their podcast Newly introduced Heights, Kelce’s brother Jason asked him about being Swift’s creative muse for The Life of a Showgirl. The tight end coyly replied, “I’m just the lucky man that gets to be, you know, the support system for Taylor while she drops one of the coolest albums that I’ve ever listened to, that the world’s seen. I’m excited for her. I’m happy for her. Everything seems to have gone perfectly, all this planning.”.

He detailed what it was like watching her make the album, revealing that he got to listen to it before it was released. “You see it from start to finish,” he mentioned. “She started this thing in the middle of her [Eras] Tour in Europe. To see it all unfold and come together and her connect the dots—from the strategic planning to how the album was all going to look—then to listen to the music, and everything comes together and her finally getting that 12th song and being like ‘I think it’s done.’.

Industry observers note that “From that point on, it’s like her and her label are just working their ass off to make this one of the biggest releases of all time,” he added. “I’m just happy as hell for it because she’s happy with it. She’s proud of this and obviously I’m proud of her for going through the hoops to live out her dreams.”.

#7993. The Art of Breakfast: What American Hotels Can Learn From Europe

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (786 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Elle ↗ Open Full Page

The Art of Breakfast: What American Hotels Can Learn From Europe

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, there are few things more revealing about a hotel than its breakfast.
  • According to recent reports, at Gstaad Palace, the grand Swiss hotel, breakfast is, like everything else, a dignified affair.
  • “Guests should feel like they are in their castle or palace, and they should be welcomed like it’s their house and it’s their best friends serving them,” said Andrea Scherz, general manager, whose family has owned the hotel since 1947.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there are few things more revealing about a hotel than its breakfast. A property can have beautiful rooms and a marble-clad lobby, but the morning meal is where hospitality is really put to the test. And while American hotels have become very good at building elaborate breakfast buffets, there is often something missing: the sense that anyone has given the experience that much thought. Too often, guests are greeted with scrambled eggs under a heat lamp, a few slices of wet bacon, and a $38 bill. In Europe, meanwhile, breakfast can involve silver cake stands, homemade jams, excellent coffee, and a real sense of place.

According to recent reports, at Gstaad Palace, the grand Swiss hotel, breakfast is, like everything else, a dignified affair. The buffet is beautiful but not extravagant, and the selection spans house-made juices, jams, and pastries, eggs cooked to order, and service that runs more smoothly than a Patek Philippe. And yet, despite the formality of the space, the experience feels wonderfully relaxed.

“Guests should feel like they are in their castle or palace, and they should be welcomed like it’s their house and it’s their best friends serving them,” said Andrea Scherz, general manager, whose family has owned the hotel since 1947. “It shouldn’t be a procedure.”.

In a recent development, scherz recently had breakfast at an American hotel that left him less than impressed. The food wasn’t necessarily the problem—it was the little things that were missing, the gestures that make a guest feel looked after rather than processed. A hostess took his name, checked it off a list, and asked him to wait while she set a particular table, despite there being an abundance of available tables already set. It was nearly half an hour before he was sipping his humble cappuccino. “They didn’t go the extra mile; they didn’t even go the extra meter,” he recalled.

That gets to the heart of what American hotels often get wrong about the most important meal of the day: they confuse abundance with luxury. More eggs, more bacon, more potatoes—but bigger isn’t always better. “Great breakfast is often about something less complicated,” remarked Nick Hatsatouris, owner at Caffé Tusk, a European-style café inside the Evelyn Hotel in Newly introduced York City. “A great breakfast is a simple menu with quality ingredients, the ritual of the service, and the atmosphere of the room.”.

In a recent development, there’s also the question of price. In the United States, breakfast is frequently an additional à la carte charge, even at hotels where the room rate can feel steep. At most European hotels, the charge is folded into the room rate in advance; for guests booking through a travel advisor, it is often waived.

Industry observers note that “For American hotels, I think the lesson is about more than including breakfast in the rate,” stated Amy Brandwein, the James Beard Award-nominated chef-owner of Washington, D.C.’s Centrolina. “It’s about recognizing breakfast as an essential part of hospitality and an opportunity to express a hotel’s identity, its connection to local producers, and its commitment to the guest’s well-being.”.

Recent findings suggest that beyond price, the best hotel breakfasts in Europe also reflect where guests are. At Gleneagles in Scotland, for instance, the Scullery puts a distinctly Scottish spin on the morning buffet with local charcuterie, house-made sausages and haggis, and freshly prepared eggs and pancakes. There’s a Bloody Mary station, too, as well as undeniably cozy and humble Scottish porridge. Adare Manor in Ireland serves its breakfast of Irish breads, cheeses, and hot dishes in a 132-foot-long gallery. And at Passalacqua on Lake Como, guests can take breakfast in the garden or beneath frescoed ceilings, with fresh fruit grown in the property’s gardens, eggs from the property’s own chickens, and 11 varieties of regional cakes arranged on silver tiered stands.

Of course, not every hotel needs a sprawling buffet or a kitchen turning out elaborate dishes. Smaller, more thoughtful changes can go a long way.

Brandwein remembers European breakfasts for their balance: beautiful cappuccinos, whole-grain breads, oats, flaxseeds, fresh fruit, and excellent local honey. “I find the typical American hotel breakfast rather heavy and unimaginative,” she remarked, pointing to the usual emphasis on eggs, potatoes, bacon, and sausage. She would like to see more whole grains, fresh produce, and lighter preparations. The ingredients don’t need to be complicated; in fact, the simpler they are, the better. Quality and presentation go a long way.

A hotel breakfast doesn’t need 40 items on a buffet or a pastry chef working through the night. It needs good coffee, something fresh and local, and a staff who seem happy to have you there.

#7987. NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson loses reelection in North Carolina

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (633 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson loses reelection in North Carolina

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (633 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson, right, here at a hearing in June, lost his reelection bid in North Carolina's 9th District.
  • Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee, has lost his race for reelection, a stinging defeat for the man charged with preserving the House majority for the GOP.
  • Hudson fell to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator who was leading  51 percent to 49 percent Thursday afternoon  when The Associated Press called the race in North Carolina’s 9th District.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson, right, here at a hearing in June, lost his reelection bid in North Carolina's 9th District. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

North Carolina Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee, has lost his race for reelection, a stinging defeat for the man charged with preserving the House majority for the GOP.

Hudson fell to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator who was leading  51 percent to 49 percent Thursday afternoon  when The Associated Press called the race in North Carolina’s 9th District.

Hudson had already conceded the race Wednesday, when it became clear that his path to victory was closing off.

“[The] voters of North Carolina’s 9th District made their choice and I respect it,” he mentioned in a statement. “Since 2013 I’ve worked for North Carolina families. That includes the soldiers and families at Fort Bragg, who sacrifice more for this country than most people will ever know.”.

Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose his seat during a midterm election this decade. In 2022, Latest York Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney lost reelection while serving as chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

Republicans across North Carolina experienced devastating losses on election night. As of Thursday afternoon, Democrats had also flipped the seats of Reps. Addison McDowell, Brad Knott and Tim Moore, as well as the open seat of retiring Rep. Chuck Edwards. The races for five other GOP-held seats remain uncalled, while Democratic Rep. Don Davis was reelected despite being targeted for defeat under a new GOP-drawn congressional map. Republicans also lost control of the North Carolina House and lost seats in the state Senate.

In a recent development, north Carolina’s 9th District, which includes the Eastern Piedmont region and the Fayetteville area, was far from the House battlefield for much of the midterm cycle. President Donald Trump carried the seat by 16 points in 2024, according to calculations by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, and Hudson won a seventh term the same year by nearly 19 points. Hudson also held a financial advantage over Ojeda, raising $4.2 million to Ojeda’s $2.9 million through mid-October.

But in the waning weeks of the campaign, signs of Republican concern grew and Hudson’s campaign began spending on ads.

Ojeda was first elected to the West Virginia Senate in 2016. He ran for the U.S. House two years later as a Trump-voting Democrat but lost that race to Republican Carol Miller. He then briefly ran for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination and also challenged GOP Sen. Shelley Moore Capito later that cycle but lost in the Democratic primary.

Ojeda moved to North Carolina in 2020, he told CityView, a local magazine, and he announced his challenge to Hudson last year.

Recent findings suggest that throughout the campaign, he attacked the incumbent over his support for Trump’s agenda, particularly the war in Iran. Ojeda is a retired Army major and the district is home to Fort Bragg, the nation’s largest Army base by population, where the Democrat was previously stationed for more than a decade.

Recent findings suggest that “We did the impossible,’’ Ojeda told supporters Tuesday night. “We took on the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, a man with political connections, the billionaire donors, and the entire Washington establishment standing beside him.”.

Hudson, 55, is finishing his seventh term in the House and his second term as NRCC chair. He had no primary opponent this year and had grown used to winning reelection by comfortable margins.

As a legislator, Hudson focused much of his policy agenda on health issues such as federal pandemic preparedness programs. He serves on the House Energy and Commerce Committee and chairs the panel's Communications and Technology Subcommittee.

As a shopping editor who tracks prices on Apple products all year, I have high standards. Truth be told, Apple tech deals have had some highs and lows this year: some items reached their lowest prices ever during major sale moments like Prime Day, while others (I’m looking at you, Labor Day deals!) have been less than impressive. Now that Amazon’s 12-day Black Friday sale is here, I’m creating an official guide to the iPad deals you should shop now...and which are worth waiting a little longer for.

According to recent reports, I’m forecasting steeper deals during the day of Black Friday (November 27), but that doesn’t mean you’re doomed to wait. Ahead, you’ll find an updated guide to all the iPad models on sale right now:.

So far, the best Black Friday iPad deal up for grabs is $100 off the iPad Mini. This small but mighty tablet is powered by the speedy A17 chip, with a 12MP camera that can capture 4K videos. It’s compact at 7.7 inches tall and weighs less than a pound (0.66 pounds, to be exact), which makes it the perfect size to toss in your purse for on-the-go streaming and note-taking.

Though this is the steepest iPad deal thus far, it still pales in comparison to last year’s discount. This exact model was a record-low $349 during last year’s Black Friday sale, so there’s a good chance it’ll get even cheaper in the days to come.

You can also score $100 off the latest iPad Air model. It’s powered by the M4 chip, which boasts advanced graphics and a powerful processing system that multitasks with ease—whether you’re editing videos, jotting down notes, or creating presentation slides. When paired with the Magic Keyboard, it can function more like a laptop than a typical tablet. It’s available in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes, with storage ranging from 512GB to 1TB.

Price-wise, this isn’t the best discount I’ve ever seen. It’s been on sale for as low as $519, a whopping $130 cheaper than its current sale price. Even though it’s the steepest deal available right now, there’s a strong chance that it drops in price on Black Friday.

Another iPad deal I’m keeping an eye on? The 11th-generation iPad, which was released in 2025. Although its current $50 discount isn’t particularly impressive, I saw it drop below $300 during last year’s Black Friday sale. I recommend holding out just a little longer to get a better deal.

Industry observers note that compared to the iPad Air, this model sacrifices some processing power for a more affordable price point. The A16 chip is better suited for tasks like scrolling your TikTok feed, flipping through your e-book library, and streaming the Love Is Blind finale, so it’s a great option if you prefer using your iPad in recreational settings. It comes in three storage sizes—128, 256, and 512GB—with the best discount on the 128GB model.

Industry observers note that all in all, the iPad deals available right now aren’t worth writing home about—but don’t despair! These deals can literally change in an instant, and I’m predicting that prices will become comparable to last year’s Black Friday sale if you’re willing to wait until next week. #7972. Latest Update: At the Races: After the deluge

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2157 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: At the Races: After the deluge

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2157 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tuesday’s rout by Democrats has led one group dedicated to electing more Republican women to Congress to warn of a “crisis-level decline” of female GOP members on Capitol Hill.
  • Danielle Barrow, the president of Women for Women Action Fund, drew parallels between this week’s results and the 2018 blue wave.
  • “After 2018, when Republicans lost 40 seats and elected only one latest Republican woman, the party made a real commitment to recruiting and investing in women – and it worked,” Barrow said in a statement Wednesday, adding that women accounted for 11 of the 15 House seats the GOP picked up in the 2020 election.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tuesday’s rout by Democrats has led one group dedicated to electing more Republican women to Congress to warn of a “crisis-level decline” of female GOP members on Capitol Hill.

Danielle Barrow, the president of Women for Women Action Fund, drew parallels between this week’s results and the 2018 blue wave.

“After 2018, when Republicans lost 40 seats and elected only one latest Republican woman, the party made a real commitment to recruiting and investing in women – and it worked,” Barrow said in a statement Wednesday, adding that women accounted for 11 of the 15 House seats the GOP picked up in the 2020 election. But she cautioned that the party needs to sustain that focus across election cycles.

“Republicans cannot only make this investment after a wipeout election and abandon it when things improve,” she noted. “It is time for party leaders to treat this as a permanent strategy, not a crisis response.”.

The ranks of House Republican women won’t plummet to as low as after the 2018 elections, when the caucus had just 13 female members. At least 18 Republican women have won House races so far, according to The Associated Press, and two others are leading as of Thursday afternoon. The conference is likely to see two newly introduced female members: Florida’s Sydney Gruters, the wife of RNC Chairman Joe Gruters, and Washington state’s Amanda McKinney, who holds a comfortable lead as votes continue to be counted.

Still, those figures are worlds apart from House Democrats, whose caucus will have more than 100 women next year.

Industry observers note that “We have always known that when women run, women win,” Florida Rep. Lois Frankel, chair of the member-led Elect Democratic Women PAC, mentioned in a statement Wednesday.

Those incoming latest members span the ideological range of the party, including progressives from New York and California who scored big primary wins this summer, to more moderate Democrats who flipped seats in Virginia and Pennsylvania.

It has been revealed that house Democrats had set a public goal this cycle to push their female membership past 100. Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who is retiring at the end of the year, noted electing Democratic women had been her “passion” since she joined the House in 1987.

“We made a decision to make more room for women at the tables of power – and generations of candidates, organizers and supporters have carried that work forward,” she said.

It has been revealed that blue breakthrough: Democrats flipped the House and Senate this week, giving the party one of its biggest nights in decades. On the Senate side, they wrested seats from Republicans in Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and Ohio, while finally flipping Maine. Meanwhile, on the House side, Democrats were on track to not just win every race rated a Toss-up by Inside Elections but also pick up seats in deep-red territory that weren’t considered competitive until late in the cycle. Mary Ellen and Daniela summed up their initial election night takeaways, including how Democratic moderates and progressives both cheered the results and why many of Trump’s picks flopped at the ballot box.

Not going anywhere: The top Senate Democrat, Charles E. Schumer of New York, is confident he will be elected majority leader by his caucus, especially after the party’s resounding midterm wins. Several of his incoming members have promised to support others, our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports, but the reality is there’s no real plausible alternative. Schumer’s own seat is up in 2028.

According to recent reports, redistricting rout: Republicans’ redistricting gambit hasn’t paid off as they’d hoped, the latest election results show, with the GOP appearing poised to flip only a handful of redrawn seats. Democratic incumbents who sought reelection from their reconfigured seats appeared poised to all win, although the race for Rep. Darren Soto’s Central Florida seat remained uncalled as of Thursday afternoon.

Taking the chair: Among the bruising defeats that North Carolina Republicans suffered this week was National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson’s loss to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator. Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose reelection this decade after New York’s Sean Patrick Maloney , who lost in 2022 while serving as the DCCC chair.

New senators: The incoming Senate Democratic class includes a returning senator, a former governor, two lieutenant governors and a congressman, a notable amount of governing experience. Meanwhile, five Republican House members are moving across the Rotunda after winning open Senate seats.

Member-to-governor pipeline grows: Five newly elected governors will be departing Capitol Hill to become the top executive of their state or territory, Savannah reports. Additionally, two former members who also served in the Biden administration were elected governor, though a trio of House Republicans fell short in their gubernatorial bids.

Comeback season: Roll Call’s Nick Eskow reports on the former members who are poised to return to the House or Senate next year, with at least seven winning comeback bids Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that the firsts: Several candidates made history this week with their elections to Congress or the governorships of their state. Roll Call’s Andrew Menezes rounds up the milestone wins.

Sources indicate that D.C. in the House: Robert White, D.C.’s newly elected nonvoting delegate, told our colleague Nina Heller that he looks to lobby fellow Democrats next year to support D.C. statehood. A potential selling point: The party could tackle affordability concerns better with two Democratic senators from the deep-blue District, he noted.

Industry observers note that keeping count: As of 4:30 p.m. Thursday, Democrats had flipped 42 seats in the House and seven in the Senate, according to the AP. Republicans have so far picked up two House seats, both through redistricting. Twenty-eight House contests and two Senate races (Alaska and Mississippi) remain uncalled as of publication time. Check out Roll Call’s results tracker for updates as the races are called.

It has been revealed that indie losses: Independent Senate hopefuls running in deep-red states did not find success on Tuesday, even in races without a Democrat on the ballot. In Nebraska, former union leader Dan Osborn came up short in his second Senate bid. In Idaho, former state legislator Todd Achilles failed to dislodge Sen. Jim Risch, while Navy veteran Brian Bengs couldn’t topple South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds. In Montana, where the Democratic nominee did not drop out, former university president Seth Bodnar lost to Republican Kurt Alme. On the House side, Alaska GOP Rep. Nick Begich comfortably leads commercial fisherman Bill Hill, though below the 50 percent threshold needed to avoid a ranked-choice runoff. With votes still being counted, the AP had yet to call the race at publication time.

According to recent reports, not just Congress: The blue wave that broke Republican majorities on Capitol Hill also washed over state legislatures. Democrats are poised to hold new majorities in 12 legislative chambers, including the North Carolina House and Texas House, according to the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, although some results aren’t official yet. The party also won governing trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Meanwhile, in blue states, Democrats tightened their grip on government: In Rhode Island, Republicans are on track to hold just 10 seats in the entire 113-member legislature, while next door in Connecticut, the 36-seat Senate could have as few as three GOP members.

Blame game: As Republicans take stock of what went wrong for them in the midterms, Vice President JD Vance was quick to point to the Iran conflict as an insurmountable albatross. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance stated in a lengthy X post. “If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. … But everyone knows why we lost.”.

It has been revealed that but the tariffs: A pair of Republican former senators, Arizona’s Jeff Flake and Pennsylvania’s Patrick J. Toomey, both also urged their party to focus on the impact of Trump’s tariff policies. “Arbitrary and capricious tariffs directly raised costs for all American consumers,” Toomey wrote Wednesday on X. “Many voted for Democrats yesterday.”.

In a recent development, staying put: Pennsylvania Rep. Brendan F. Boyle indicates he will remain in the House, where he’s poised to become the next Budget Committee chair, rather than launch a Democratic primary challenge to Sen. John Fetterman next cycle.

It has been revealed that bayh Bayh Bayh: A third generation of Indiana’s famed Bayh family won political office this week, with Beau Bayh’s election as secretary of state. Bayh, a Marine Corps veteran, follows in the footsteps of his father, Evan Bayh, who won the same post 40 years ago before going on to serve as governor and senator, and his late grandfather, Birch Bayh, who won three terms in the Senate. Indiana Democrats had a breakthrough election this week, defeating GOP Rep. Victoria Spartz, winning a second statewide office, unseating the speaker and breaking the GOP supermajority in the state House.

It has been revealed that A win and a loss: Nebraska Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts won reelection, but his wife, Democrat Susanne Shore, lost a special election for a seat on University of Nebraska Board of Regents, which governs the university system. Shore, who lost to a fellow Democrat in the officially nonpartisan race, was making her first bid for elective office.

It has been revealed that bans on the ballot: Voters in Arizona, Nebraska and Washington state have approved new measures barring transgender athletes from participating in girls sports. A similar proposal in Colorado also appears likely to pass, although the AP had yet to call it as of publication time.

Industry observers note that roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections shares 15 initial lessons from the midterm elections, from the president’s “political mortality” to candidate quality and the power of personal brands. And, Nathan writes, as bad a night as it was for Republicans, it could have been even worse.

As Maine goes: The Newly introduced York Times caught up with with Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her bid for a sixth term in Maine. Collins, who had survived tough cycles before, spoke of getting “caught up in the Trump tsunami” and how she finally had her “Margaret Chase Smith moment.”.

“These are extinction-level numbers”: Texas Monthly sat down for an interview with former state House Speaker Dade Phelan, who anticipated a down-ballot GOP rout but not the full extent of it. “MAGA needs to be dead,’’ said the Republican, who led the push to impeach state Attorney General Ken Paxton in 2023 and then was targeted for defeat by Trump. He opted against reelection this year.

Corruption a top glitch: The Associated Press reported that its 2026 voter poll found corruption at the top of the list of concerns for voters who helped sweep Democrats into power on Capitol Hill.

Tar Heeled: Among the states where Republicans suffered their biggest defeats Tuesday, perhaps none was more stunning than North Carolina, where they've so far lost five U.S. House seats and are trailing in one another and lost control of the state House. The (Raleigh) News & Observer looks at how maps “designed to deliver strong Republican majorities [failed] so spectacularly at that goal.”.

According to recent reports, support and discord: Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s sharply critical views toward Israel roiled the Jewish community in Michigan. But exit polling suggests most Jewish voters backed him, albeit in smaller numbers than they might have had a different Democrat run, Religion News Service reports.

That's how many House districts won by Trump in 2024 have been called for Democratic candidates by the AP as of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time on Thursday.

Twenty-eight additional Trump-won districts remain uncalled at publication time, and Democrats are at the moment leading in eight of those races.

The figures stand in sharp contrast to the start of the cycle, when there were just 13 House Democrats in districts that backed Trump in 2024.

Since then, several Republican-led states redrew their congressional maps in an effort to increase the number of Trump-won districts and improve their party’s chances of holding the House.

In a recent development, in large part, this effort appears to have backfired in 2026, with the Democratic wave cresting high enough to wash over dozens of Trump-won districts. Twenty-one of the 52 Democratic wins so far have come in states that redrew their congressional lines: Texas (six Trump-won seats), North Carolina (six), Ohio (five), Florida (three) and Alabama (one).

Congressional Republicans are holding leadership elections next week as they transition from the majority to the minority party. Speaker Mike Johnson is not seeking his conference’s top post, setting up a clash to be the next House minority leader. On the Senate side, South Dakota’s John Thune hopes to continue leading his party in the chamber.

Industry observers note that if there’s one rookie move that negates all the time, effort, and creativity that went into a design project, it’s settling for mediocre photography. “The last place you want to cut a corner is in the photography because that’s your calling card,” notes industry-leading photographer Douglas Friedman (who was featured in a trade talk with AD PRO). “That’s going to sell you for the next project and everything after that.”.

In other words, whether you’re shooting a contemporary penthouse, historic mansion, or cozy cottage, the right interior photographers can make or break the way your space is remembered. Light, perspective, mood; the perfect photo combines all three, not just creating a visual record, but also telling a story in a single image. And while it can be daunting to pick just the right photographer to showcase your work, AD PRO is here to make that easier. We tapped AD’s photo editors—the individuals who commission, sift through, and select the thousands of amazing images we publish each year—for their recommendations of up-and-coming interior photographers across the US and beyond.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve organized the 180-plus talents they selected by region, so you can find one who works near you and is adept at capturing the changing light in the high desert, a snow-covered mountain, or palm-tree-lined island—wherever you find yourself working. But do keep in mind that most of these exceptional interior photographers are happy to travel, shooting stunning interiors the world over. Several even work from multiple home bases, so it’s worth clicking on every regional story while looking for your perfect match. Once you find the right collaborator to commemorate and celebrate your work, you’ll make unforgettable images together.

Sources indicate that find your next creative collaborator using the AD PRO Sourcebook. Start exploring top interior photographers, stylists, decorative painters, millworkers, and more now.

Recent findings suggest that grand staircases. Cozy breakfast nooks. Color-drenched walls. All-white living rooms. You name it, these pros below have shot it—in daylight and darkness—maximizing views of the park or the coast, the backyard or the city street far below. Their images are portraits of homes, capturing a space’s personality and highlighting the talents of its designer.

Newly introduced Orleans. Charleston. Nashville. Miami. Some of the nation’s most distinctive cities are found in the Southeast, each one celebrated for its unique architecture, music, cuisine, and mix of cultures. The photographers listed below capture the personality of each vibrant city—not to mention the more rural beauty of the lakefronts, coastline, and countryside in between them. Maximizing natural light and architectural details, these photographers imbue their home photos with Southern hospitality. Read on for AD-approved interior photographers in the Southeast.

Sources indicate that the central states of this nation have given us a lot to be grateful for when it comes to architecture and interior design. There’s the Prairie School and the Chicago School of Architecture, not to mention American Bauhaus and Midwestern Modern. Luckily, the region has also produced stellar interior photographers in the Midwest to capture all the glory.

In a recent development, many of the shutterbugs on these pages shoot commercial projects and fine art as well as interiors, capturing light-filled living rooms and cozy bedrooms alike. Often working with natural light, these interior photographers use perspective to make the most of wide-open spaces as well as cozy apartments. One look at their work—whether it’s intimate or expansive—and you’ll see these photographers are more than Midwestern nice. They’re Midwestern marvelous.

In a recent development, from the blinding sunshine in Texas to the glare off the snow in Utah, interior photographers in the Southwest have a distinct set of challenges to work with as they strive to give the homes they shoot as much majesty and drama as the landscape that surrounds them. The pros on this list more than rise to that Texas-sized challenge, whether they’re shooting dens in the desert or living rooms by the lake.

Whether the view outside the window is of the Santa Monica pier or the peak of Mount Rainier, the homes photographed by AD’s most trusted interior photographers on the West Coast always end up looking as impressive as the scenery that surrounds them. While many of them are bicoastal or even work internationally, these pros are experts on shooting West Coast interiors. And they’re not just leading lights in the field of interior photography; many of these artists excel in travel, landscape, or portrait photography as well—but each one of these photographers is guaranteed to make a home look like a worthy setting for a Hollywood blockbuster.

They jet around the globe, camera in hand, capturing expansive views from clifftop villas and intimate reading nooks in private homes. The international interior photographers on these pages don’t just record living spaces; they tell stories and create moods, turning their eyes to details such as the light streaming through a red curtain or a marble statue waiting to welcome guests into a villa’s entryway. Each image is infused with a sense of place and the spirit of the people who pass through it. Being our semi-regular weekly survey of what’s going down in the several states where, as we know, the real work of governmentin’ gets done and where the rifleman’s stalking the sick and the lame.

Our semi-regular weekly survey this week is very heavy on people who want to build things of which many other people want no part.

We begin in the Commonwealth. (God save it!) South from Worcester on Route 146 lies the charming town of Sutton. Back in the day, Sutton’s Pleasant Valley Country Club was a regular stop on the PGA and LPGA Tours. (The last PGA event at the course was in 1998.) There also was a drive-in that showed films of ... ahem ... a sophisticated nature. Anyway, I used to drive through Sutton on my way to my job in the state forest. Route 146 got progressively more rural the further you got from Worcester. Now, Bob Kraft, the owner of the New England Patriots, would like to drop a data center on the town. From CBS News:.

The idea of dropping a power-draining, water-gulping ten-building campus on a place as small as Sutton is exactly why data centers have become the hot-button local problem all over the country. It is sheer oligarchical bullying over which the country has raised its hackles. This would be the fourth-largest data center in the United States. And, as WGBH points out, some sports oligarchs are leading the parade on these projects, which is reason enough to give every one of these projects a serious side-eye.

It’s good to be rich in this country. You may not have noticed.

Elsewhere, Erik Loomis of LG&M points us to another oligarch’s dreamscape, this one in the beleaguered state of West Virginia. From The Washington Post:.

Industry observers note that pause for a moment and roll that business-school candy corn around in your mouth for a second. A Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus. A glow-in-the-dark euphemism for the good people of Jefferson County.

We’re back in the three-card-monte game of “Jerbs!” that we all had to play in relation to our old friend the Keystone XL pipeline. We have to be careful how many of these jobs are temporary construction jobs and how many are the strippers who come to town to entertain them.

(Jesus, Louisiana? Really? Are you prepared to move aside one of your eleventy-million chemical plants and refineries to make room for nuclear-waste disposal facilities? Take a knee on this one, okay?).

You mean communities are anxious about becoming repositories for poisonous waste with a half-life of up to 24,000 years? What is wrong with people anyway?

It has been revealed that energetic local community activism on issues like these was one of the most underrated sources of energy behind the historic Democratic sweep two weeks ago. People are starting to enjoy fighting the power again.

Industry observers note that in that spirit, we conclude, as is our custom, in the great state of Oklahoma, whence Blog Official Overseas Operative Friedman of the Algarve brings us yet another story about toxic waste. From Tulsa Flyer:.

Delightful. And who was it that tried to kill Bell Cow Lake?

It is going to take decades to get clear of all the damage these clowns have done, if we even can, which I doubt more seriously every day.

This is your democracy, America. Cherish it.

The real dustup came over the nomination of one T. Elliot Gaiser, the head of the DOJ’s Office of Legal Counsel, to a seat on a federal district court in Texas. The next two months are going to be such fun.

#7960. As Democrats look to next era, the veto and the filibuster await

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1507 w)
